# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction
Heart failure (HF) remains a major global health burden with high morbidity and mortality despite major advances in guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) [1, 2]. Device-based therapies, most notably cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), have revolutionized the management of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [3]. However, CRT is indicated only for patients with a wide QRS complex (typically $\ge 130$ ms), leaving approximately 70% of symptomatic HF patients with a narrow QRS complex ineligible [3, 4]. For this substantial cohort, cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) has emerged as an innovative, device-based treatment option that improves functional status, quality of life, and exercise tolerance [5, 6].

## Mechanism of Action
Unlike pacing therapies that trigger myocardial contraction, CCM involves the delivery of high-voltage, biphasic, non-excitatory electrical signals during the absolute refractory period of the cardiac action potential [6, 7]. Because these signals are delivered when the myocardium is incapable of initiating a new action potential, they do not alter the activation sequence or heart rate [7, 8]. Instead, CCM exerts its effects on a cellular level. Locally, it enhances calcium cycling by upregulating the expression and phosphorylation of sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase 2a (SERCA2a) and phospholamban, while downregulating the sodium-calcium exchanger (NCX) [8, 9]. Over time, these molecular modifications reverse the "fetal gene program" characteristic of heart failure, leading to systemic, beneficial left ventricular (LV) remodeling and increased myocardial contractility without a concomitant increase in myocardial oxygen consumption [9, 10].

## Clinical Trials and Efficacy
The clinical efficacy of CCM has been systematically evaluated in several multicenter clinical trials. The FIX-HF-4 trial was a randomized, double-blind crossover study that demonstrated significant improvements in exercise capacity, measured by peak oxygen consumption ($\text{VO}_2$), and quality of life in CCM-treated patients [11]. The subsequent FIX-HF-5 trial, which randomized 328 patients with NYHA class III/IV HFrEF, showed similar functional improvements [12]. A post-hoc subgroup analysis of FIX-HF-5 revealed that patients with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) between 25% and 45% derived the most pronounced benefit [13].

To confirm these findings, the FIX-HF-5C trial was conducted in patients with NYHA class III/IV HF, narrow QRS complexes, and LVEFs between 25% and 45% [14]. FIX-HF-5C met its primary endpoint, showing significant improvements in peak $\text{VO}_2$ and Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire (MLHFQ) scores, alongside a substantial reduction in the composite rate of cardiovascular mortality and HF hospitalizations [14]. Multiple meta-analyses pooling these trial data have consistently validated CCM's capacity to enhance functional capacity, increase 6-minute walk distance (6MWD), and reduce HF-related hospitalizations [15, 16, 17].

## Real-World Evidence and Long-Term Outcomes
Beyond randomized trials, real-world registries have confirmed the safety and long-term durability of CCM. The Cardiac Contractility Modulation Active Use Registry (CC-REG) demonstrated that CCM is associated with a significant reduction in long-term mortality and HF hospitalization rates compared to predicted outcomes, with benefits sustained for several years [18]. Other long-term observational studies have corroborated these survival benefits and shown a low incidence of device-related complications [19, 20]. Clinical experience has also demonstrated that CCM is safe and highly compatible with implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs), showing no adverse electrical interference [21, 22]. Furthermore, emerging evidence suggests that CCM may also offer clinical benefits for patients with heart failure and mid-range or preserved ejection fraction (HFmrEF/HFpEF) by improving diastolic relaxation and clinical symptoms [23, 24].

## Patient Selection and Clinical Guidelines
CCM is delivered via the Optimizer device (Impulse Dynamics, Stuttgart, Germany), which is typically implanted subcutaneously with two leads positioned in the right ventricular septum [25, 26]. Currently, the 2021 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines recommend considering CCM in patients with NYHA class III/IV HFrEF, LVEF 25–45%, and QRS duration <120 ms who remain symptomatic despite GDMT, to improve exercise capacity and quality of life [2]. Similarly, the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guidelines highlight CCM as an emerging device-based therapy for symptomatic HFrEF with narrow QRS [1]. To ensure optimal outcomes, patient selection should focus on those who are stable on optimal medical therapy but continue to experience lifestyle-limiting symptoms [27, 28]. Multidisciplinary heart failure teams play a vital role in identifying eligible candidates, managing post-implantation follow-up, and optimizing device parameters [29, 30].

## Conclusion
Cardiac contractility modulation represents a major therapeutic advancement for a large subset of symptomatic heart failure patients who are ineligible for CRT. By targeting cellular calcium handling and reversing pathological gene expression, CCM safely improves functional capacity, quality of life, and clinical outcomes. As clinical guidelines and real-world experience continue to evolve, CCM is poised to become an increasingly integral component of device-based heart failure management.
